x-m-fill-a-01.title: If the total is right, is the table right too?
x-m-fill-a-01.topic: Data and chances: sorting, counting, and showing in a table
x-m-fill-a-01.goal: When showing sorted-and-counted results in a table, understand why a fix that only matches the total can't be trusted, and describe how to recheck each cell.
x-m-fill-a-01.material:
16 classmates were asked their favorite fruit. Each person chose only one, and the answers were written on the board in the order they were chosen.
strawberry, mandarin, mandarin, grape, strawberry, strawberry, mandarin, grape, mandarin, strawberry, grape, mandarin, strawberry, mandarin, strawberry, strawberry
Sewoon counted these and made a table.
[Table] strawberry 7 / mandarin 5 / grape 3 / total 15
x-m-fill-a-01.thinking.0: Find a fix that has no basis in the work
x-m-fill-a-01.thinking.1: Think of cases where it can be wrong even if the total is the same
x-m-fill-a-01.prereq.0: Sorting things or names by kind and counting them one by one
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.prompt: This is Sewoon's thinking about fixing the table. Choose the line that has a place that is hard to trust.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into whether it is the result of recounting the board or just a guess.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.hint.1: Look for whether any line checks that the cell you changed was really the wrong one.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.line.1: Adding all the cells of the table gives 7+5+3=15.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.line.2: 15 is 1 less than 16, so I must have missed one person somewhere.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.line.3: Grape is the smallest, so I probably missed it while counting. I'll change the grape cell from 3 to 4.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.line.4: The fixed table has 7+5+4=16, so it is right now.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s1.explain: Line 4 chose which cell to fix by guessing, without recounting the board. Line 5 said the table is right just because the total became 16, but you can make the total the same even when other cells are wrong. In fact, if you count the board, mandarin is 6 people. Lines 2 and 3 are fine, because they found the clue that someone is missing.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.prompt: What is the most trustworthy way to find the wrong cell?
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.hint.0: Does a total that doesn't match tell you where the mistake is, or only that there is a mistake?
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think of a way to separate what you have already counted from what you haven't counted yet while you count.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.r.c: You thought that marking items one by one by kind while counting can prevent missing or double counting.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.o.d: Show the table to another friend and ask if it is right
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.r.d: That depends on someone else's judgment. There is also a way to check directly with the data on the board.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s2.explain: If you recount by kind while marking what you have counted, you can find directly which cell was wrong. The total is only a signal that 'something is wrong somewhere'; it does not tell you where.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.prompt: When you recounted, mandarin was 6 people. What would you say if Sewoon says, 'If the total is 16, the table is always right'? Give a numerical example of a wrong table whose total is 16, and also write how to check whether a table is right.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.hint.0: Decide on just one way you could make a cell wrong, for example.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what you should do again when checking, besides adding the total again.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the wrong table you gave, the total is 16, but is it clear which cell is wrong?
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is your way of checking 'recounting the data' rather than 'calculating the total'?
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.model.0: Even if the total is 16, it can be wrong. For example, strawberry 8, mandarin 5, grape 3 has a total of 16 but a wrong cell. You should recount by crossing out one fruit at a time.
x-m-fill-a-01.s.s3.model.1: Even if the total is the same, the table can be wrong. If you wrongly count strawberry as 6 and mandarin as 7, with grape 3 the total is still 16. You have to recount the board for each cell to check.

x-m-fill-a-03.title: You can be fooled by bar height alone
x-m-fill-a-03.topic: Data and chances: bar graph scales and errors in comparison
x-m-fill-a-03.goal: Make examples to see that a bar graph whose vertical scale does not start at 0 can make a difference look bigger, and say why you should look at the scale first when reading a graph.
x-m-fill-a-03.material:
Minseo's class library lent out 90 books in March and 95 books in April. The same data was drawn as two bar graphs.
Graph 가: The vertical scale starts at 0 books, and one step is 10 books. The March bar and the April bar look almost the same height.
Graph 나: The vertical scale starts at 80 books, and one step is 5 books. The March bar is 2 steps tall and the April bar is 3 steps tall.
Minseo looked at graph 나 and said, 'The April bar is 1.5 times as tall as the March bar, so the books lent in April were 1.5 times as many too!'
x-m-fill-a-03.thinking.0: Tell apart how a graph looks from the actual numbers
x-m-fill-a-03.thinking.1: Make an example that meets conditions
x-m-fill-a-03.thinking.2: Explain the reason for a way of reading
x-m-fill-a-03.prereq.0: Reading the vertical scale of a bar graph
x-m-fill-a-03.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of two numbers
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting thought about what Minseo said?
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.hint.0: Read the actual number of books for March and April from the scales of both graphs.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.hint.1: How many books is the lowest scale mark of graph 나?
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.o.a: Graph 가 and graph 나 are different data, so they can't be compared
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.r.a: The two graphs show the same 90 books and 95 books. You saw them as different data.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.o.b: The bar height is 1.5 times, so the books lent are 1.5 times too
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.r.b: You read the ratio of bar heights directly as the ratio of the number of books. You did not check where the scale starts.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.o.c: The scale starts at 80, so the difference looks bigger than it really is
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.r.c: You thought of how the bars look and the actual numbers separately.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.o.d: Graph 나, which has smaller steps, is more trustworthy
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.r.d: Smaller steps don't make it more accurate. First check where the scale starts.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s1.explain: March is 90 books and April is 95 books, an increase of 5 books. Graph 나 looks as if the part below 80 books was cut off, so the ratio of bar heights is different from the ratio of the number of books.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.prompt: For a bar graph whose scale starts at s books, not 0, make two examples where the number of books actually went up by 10 or less, but the April bar looks at least 2 times as tall as the March bar. (March is a books, April is b books, the scale starts at s books, and the bar heights are a-s and b-s respectively.)
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.hint.0: If the scale starts at 80, only the part above 80 is drawn as the bar. Find the bar heights for March and April.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.hint.1: Work out how close the scale start must be to the number of books in March for the April bar to be 2 times the March bar.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.var.s: The number where the vertical scale starts (books)
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The scale starts at a number other than 0, and the March bar is visible.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The scale start must be a natural number greater than 0 and less than the number of books in March.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.ok.c2: April has more than March, by 10 books or less.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.fail.c2: April must be more than March, and the increase in books must be 10 or less.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The April bar is at least 2 times as tall as the March bar.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The April bar is not 2 times as tall as the March bar.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.explain: For example, with 90 books in March and 100 books in April and a scale starting at 80 books, the bar heights are 10 and 20, so it looks like 2 times, but in fact the number only went up by 10 books. The higher you start the scale, the bigger the difference looks.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why a bar graph like this can fool the reader, and what you should check first when you look at a graph.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the lowest scale marks of graphs 가 and 나.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write in one sentence why the same data looked different.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include 'where the scale starts'?
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the bar heights and the actual numbers look different?
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If the vertical scale does not start at 0, the difference between bars looks bigger than it really is, so you can be fooled. So when you look at a graph, first look at where the scale starts.
x-m-fill-a-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If you look at only the bar heights, it seems like it went up a lot, but that's because the scale starts at 80. So you must check the numbers on the scale and the actual number of books.

x-m-fill-a-04.title: Is the spinner game fair?
x-m-fill-a-04.topic: Data and chances: mean and chance (is it fair?)
x-m-fill-a-04.goal: Compare chances of winning by the number of sections to judge whether a rule is fair, and do not conclude it is unfair just from a difference in means over a small number of tries. Make a spinner that gives equal chances yourself.
x-m-fill-a-04.material: Jiho and Harin are playing a spinner game. The spinner is divided into 12 sections, and all sections are the same size. The sections come in three colors: red, blue, and green.
x-m-fill-a-04.thinking.0: Compare chances by the number of sections
x-m-fill-a-04.thinking.2: Revise a judgment to fit a new rule
x-m-fill-a-04.thinking.3: Make a spinner that meets conditions
x-m-fill-a-04.prereq.0: Describing a chance with words like 'certain to happen' and 'impossible,' or with numbers
x-m-fill-a-04.prereq.1: Finding the mean of several numbers
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.prompt: The rule and the data are revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thought.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many sections each person scores on.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.hint.1: Each time new data appears, compare which changed: 'the number of sections in the rule' or 'the results of the tries.'
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.info: The spinner has 5 red sections, 5 blue sections, and 2 green sections. Rule: Spin once. If red comes up, Jiho gets 1 point. If blue comes up, Harin gets 1 point. If green comes up, nobody gets a point.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Is this game fair to both players?
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Red and blue are each 5 of the 12 sections, so the chances of the two players scoring are equal. Green keeps both from scoring, so it does not affect fairness.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Red and blue have the same number of sections, so the two players have equal chances of winning
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You judged the chances by comparing the numbers of sections.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Because of the green section, both players lose out, so it's not fair
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Not scoring because of green happens to both players equally. Compare whether only one player is at a disadvantage.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The player who spins first has an advantage, so it's not fair
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: No matter who spins first, each section is equally likely to come up.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You can't know whether it's fair at all until you try it
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even without trying, you can compare chances by the number of sections.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.info: They played 3 rounds. One round is spinning the spinner 10 times. Jiho scored 6 times, 4 times, and 5 times, and Harin scored 3 times, 5 times, and 4 times.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: The means are 5 times for Jiho and 4 times for Harin. What do you think when you see these means?
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Out of 30 spins, Jiho got 15, Harin got 12, and green got 3. Even when the numbers of sections are equal, results can come out a little different over a small number of tries. If you spin more times, the difference between the two tends to get smaller.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The rule favors Jiho, who has the higher mean
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A higher mean doesn't mean the rule favors someone. You need to look, along with the number of sections, at whether the rule makes things happen equally.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Harin's mean is lower, so blue sections should be added
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You tried to change the rule right away because the results were a bit different. Think about whether a few tries are enough.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The numbers of sections are equal, so the rule is fair, and the difference in means may be just chance
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought of chance (the rule) and the results of the tries (the means) separately.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The mean has nothing to do with chance, so it's useless
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The more you try, the closer the results get to the chance. The mean is also a clue.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Jiho said, 'Let's say I also get the point when green comes up.' New rule: If red or green comes up, Jiho scores. If blue comes up, Harin scores.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The sections where Jiho scores are 5 red and 2 green, 7 sections together, and Harin has 5. When the rule changes, you have to judge again.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Red and blue have the same number of sections, so it is still fair
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You carried over the judgment from the old rule as it is. Check whether the sections where Jiho scores changed because the rule changed.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Jiho has 7 sections and Harin has 5, so Jiho has the advantage
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You counted each person's sections anew to fit the changed rule.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Green is only 2 sections, so it doesn't affect the score
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even 2 sections out of 12 make a difference in the chances.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: No matter the number of sections, the one who spins first has the advantage
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: No matter who spins first, each section is equally likely to come up.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s1.reflect: In the 2nd step, why didn't you change the rule even after seeing the difference in means? In the 3rd step, why did you revise your first judgment?
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.prompt: Keep the new rule (Jiho gets red or green, Harin gets blue) as it is, and remake the spinner with 12 sections so the two players have equal chances of scoring. Make two different spinners. (r red sections, b blue sections, g green sections. All three colors have at least 1 section, and all sections are the same size.)
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write, as expressions, the number of sections where Jiho scores and where Harin scores.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think of the 12 sections as divided into the sections where the players score and the sections where they don't.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.ok.c1: All three colors have at least 1 section.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of red, blue, and green sections must all be natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The sections do not add up to 12.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Jiho and Harin have the same number of scoring sections.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Jiho's sections (red+green) and Harin's sections (blue) are different.
x-m-fill-a-04.s.s2.explain: The sections where Jiho scores (red+green) and the sections where Harin scores (blue) must be equal, so blue must be 6 sections and red and green together must be 6 sections. Many answers are possible depending on how many red sections you use.

x-m-fill-a-06.title: Which representative value fits the purpose?
x-m-fill-a-06.topic: Data and chances: choosing a representative value from frequency tables and organized data
x-m-fill-a-06.goal: After organizing data in a frequency table, choose the representative value (mean, median, or mode) that fits the purpose, and explain the limit of the mean.
x-m-fill-a-06.material:
The monthly allowances (in 만 원) of 10 club members were organized in a frequency table.
[Frequency table] allowance 1만 원: 3 students / 2만 원: 4 students / 3만 원: 2 students / 24만 원: 1 student / total 10 students
The three values are mean 4.1만 원, median 2만 원, and mode 2만 원.
x-m-fill-a-06.thinking.0: Choose the value that fits the purpose
x-m-fill-a-06.thinking.1: Evaluate the effect of an extreme value
x-m-fill-a-06.thinking.2: Fix a statement that causes a misunderstanding
x-m-fill-a-06.prereq.0: The meaning of mean, median, and mode
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s1.prompt: If all 10 members' allowances were collected and shared out equally, which value tells how much money each person gets?
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether 'collect and share equally' uses the sum or the order.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which of the three values reflects the sum of all the data.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s1.r.c: That is the value in the exact middle. It differs from the purpose of adding up and sharing.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s1.r.d: That is one person's value. It is not the share that goes to everyone.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s1.explain: If you share the total of everyone's allowance, 41만 원, equally among 10 people, each gets 4.1만 원. For a purpose that uses the sum, the mean is right.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to introduce the club to a new member by saying, 'The allowance of our club members is about this much, usually.' Which value is the most fitting?
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s2.hint.0: Count in the frequency table how many members get less than the mean.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how the mean would change if you took out the one person with 24만 원.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s2.explain: 9 members get less than the mean (4.1만 원). The median and the mode are both 2만 원, so they are good for showing 'usual.'
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s2.acc.0: The mode 2만 원 is also the amount the most members get, so it fits showing 'usual.' In this data, the median and the mode are the same.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.prompt: A friend said, 'The mean is 4.1만 원, so most of our club gets about 4만 원 allowance.' Using this data, explain why this statement causes a misunderstanding.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.hint.0: Count how many members use more than the mean.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think roughly about how the mean would change without the 24만 원.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include how a big value like 24만 원 raised the mean?
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use numbers from the data to say how much most members really get?
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.model.0: One person has a very large 24만 원, so the mean went up. In fact, 9 members have 3만 원 or less, so most use less than the mean.
x-m-fill-a-06.s.s3.model.1: The mean got bigger because of one person who uses 24만 원, and the rest of the members use much less than the mean.

x-m-fill-a-08.title: If the means are the same, who do we send out?
x-m-fill-a-08.topic: Data and chances: interpreting variance and standard deviation
x-m-fill-a-08.goal: Interpret that two data sets with the same mean can have different spread (variance), and judge from the data which one fits which situation.
x-m-fill-a-08.material:
These are the scores of archers Jian and Doyun in their latest 5 matches.
Jian: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 points (mean 8 points, variance 2)
Doyun: 7, 8, 8, 8, 9 points (mean 8 points, variance 0.4)
The coach is thinking about who to send out in the next match.
x-m-fill-a-08.thinking.0: Tell apart what can and cannot be said from the data
x-m-fill-a-08.prereq.1: That variance and standard deviation show how spread out the data is
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that can be said to be true from this data alone.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put the two archers' scores side by side and compare how far each is from the mean of 8.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find where in the data the words 'in the future' and 'skill' come from.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.o.a: The two archers have the same mean, so their scores are spread out equally
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.r.a: Even if the means are the same, the spread is not the same. Compare how the two archers' scores look.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.o.b: Doyun's scores are gathered closer to the mean than Jian's scores
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.r.b: You read variance as spread and compared it.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.o.c: In the next match, Doyun will shoot a higher score than Jian
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.r.c: The future result can't be decided from this data. It only tells how things have been so far.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.o.d: Jian, who has the larger variance, has lower skill than Doyun
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.r.d: Variance is how spread out the scores are, not whether skill is high or low.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.o.e: The difference between the highest score and the lowest score is smaller for Doyun than for Jian
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.r.e: You looked directly at the largest and smallest values of the data and compared the spread.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s1.explain: Doyun's scores are 7 to 9 (a difference of 2), Jian's are 6 to 10 (a difference of 4), and the variances are 0.4 and 2. The future result and whether skill is high or low can't be told from this data.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.prompt: The coach is preparing two matches. (가) a match you win by shooting 9 points or more, (나) a match you win by shooting 8 points or more. Write who it would be good to send to each match, based on this data.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many times each of Jian and Doyun scored at or above the standard score of each match.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether, when the means are equal, a larger spread makes both high scores and low scores happen more often.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you decide who to send out for each of (가) and (나)?
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Instead of writing only that the means are the same, did you count how many times the standard score was reached?
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.model.0: For (가), it's Jian. In the latest 5 matches, 9 points or more happened 2 times, with 9 and 10, but Doyun has only 1. For (나), it's Doyun. 8 points or more happened 4 times, but Jian has 3.
x-m-fill-a-08.s.s2.model.1: For (가), send Jian. His 2 matches of 9 points or more are more than Doyun's 1. For (나), it's Doyun. His 4 matches of 8 points or more are more than Jian's 3.

x-m-fill-a-09.title: How does the number of cases change when order matters?
x-m-fill-a-09.topic: Data and chances: judging with the number of cases (permutations and combinations)
x-m-fill-a-09.goal: Decide whether results change with order and choose a way to count the cases, and find different situations that have the same number of cases and explain why.
x-m-fill-a-09.material: When choosing people or things for club activities, the number of cases changes depending on whether 'order matters or not.' We deal with situations where you choose from different things, and the same person is not chosen twice.
x-m-fill-a-09.thinking.0: Judge whether order changes the result
x-m-fill-a-09.thinking.1: Find several solutions that meet a condition
x-m-fill-a-09.thinking.2: Explain why the values are the same
x-m-fill-a-09.prereq.0: Experience counting the number of cases with the product rule
x-m-fill-a-09.prereq.1: How to count the ways to choose k from n different things and line them up in a row
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose every situation that must be counted as 'different results if the order of choosing or the role taken changes.'
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.hint.0: In each situation, check whether the result changes when you choose the same people (or things) and only change the order.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.hint.1: For each situation, write whether 'two results with the order changed' look like the same result.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.o.a: Choose 2 cleaning duty students from 8 different students
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.r.a: There are no roles, so who was chosen first does not change the result. Compare whether the same two people were chosen.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.o.b: Choose 3 kinds of fruit from 5 different kinds of fruit to make juice
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.r.b: Only which fruits you chose matters, and the order you chose them does not change the result.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.o.c: Choose 3 books from 4 different books and put them in a row on a bookshelf
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.r.c: You thought that which book goes in which place changes the result.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.o.d: Give 3 identical prizes, one each, to 3 of 10 students
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.r.d: They are the same prizes, so which person gets which prize can't be told apart. Only who receives matters.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.o.e: Choose 1 president and 1 vice president from 8 different students
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.r.e: You thought that even for the same two people, the result changes depending on who is president.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s1.explain: When choosing two people A and B, 'A president, B vice president' and 'B president, A vice president' are different results. For the bookshelf too, even if you choose the same 3 books, a different order of putting them is a different result. For the rest, only who (or what) was chosen matters.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter two pairs (n, k) such that the number of ways to choose k people from n different people and seat one each in k different positions is exactly 720. (2 ≤ k ≤ 6, k ≤ n ≤ 20)
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.hint.0: Try changing k to 2, 3, 4, … and decide n. Use how the value changes as n gets bigger.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.hint.1: Find how many consecutive natural numbers can be multiplied to make 720.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.var.n: Number of things to choose from, n
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.ok.c1: n and k are natural numbers in the allowed range.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.fail.c1: They must be natural numbers with 2≤k≤6 and k≤n≤20.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of cases is not 720.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why (n, k)=(6, 5) and (6, 6) both give 720.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Count how many people are left who haven't been seated after seating 5 of the 6 people.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write 6P5 and 6P6 side by side as products and compare them.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many people are left after seating 5 of the 6?
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the two numbers of cases side by side as products?
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.model.0: After choosing and seating 5 of the 6 people, the one left sits in the last position, so there is nothing more to choose. So the number of ways to seat 5 people is the same as the number of ways to seat 6 people.
x-m-fill-a-09.s.s2.because.model.1: 6P5=6×5×4×3×2 and 6P6=6×5×4×3×2×1. The values are the same because of the last factor 1. In other words, the last person is decided as the one remaining.
